theme: Israel enslaved; Moses born, hidden, and called
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 1:1-2:25. Four hundred years pass between the end of Genesis and the opening of Exodus, and the chapters you are reading cover the start of Israel’s slavery and the birth of its deliverer. Read the story with the Genesis promises in mind, and notice how often God works through small, hidden acts of courage.
settingTheScene: Genesis ended with Joseph’s family safe in Egypt. Exodus begins with a sentence that sounds like a continuation: “These are the names of the sons of Israel.” But the world has changed. Joseph’s generation has died, and the descendants of Jacob have become a great nation within Egypt’s borders. That is the fulfillment of God’s promise to Abraham to make him a great nation (Genesis 12:2). It is also the cause of Egypt’s fear. The book of Exodus is the second book of the Law, and it tells how God turned a family of slaves into a covenant people. Everything in the Bible that speaks of redemption looks back to what happens here.
observation: The people of Israel are “fruitful and increased greatly; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, so that the land was filled with them” (1:7). This echoes the creation command in Genesis 1:28.
“Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph” (1:8). He fears that Israel will join Egypt’s enemies and enslaves them (1:9-11).
The more they were oppressed, “the more they multiplied and the more they spread abroad” (1:12).
The midwives Shiphrah and Puah “feared God” and did not obey Pharaoh’s order to kill the Hebrew boys (1:17).
God “dealt well with the midwives” (1:20), and Pharaoh then commands that every newborn Hebrew boy be thrown into the Nile (1:22).
A Levite woman hides her baby son for three months, and then puts him in a basket among the reeds (2:1-3). The word for “basket” is the same word used for Noah’s ark.
Pharaoh’s daughter finds him, takes pity, and names him Moses, “because I drew him out of the water” (2:10). His sister Miriam arranges for his own mother to nurse him (2:7-9).
Moses, as an adult, kills an Egyptian who is beating a Hebrew, and flees to Midian when it becomes known (2:11-15).
In Midian, he marries Zipporah and has a son named Gershom, “I have been a sojourner in a foreign land” (2:21-22).
“God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob. God saw the people of Israel, and God knew” (2:24-25).
interpretation:
The opening chapters of Exodus are told in a quiet way. God is not named as acting until the last verses of chapter 2. Until then, the story is carried by people: a frightened king, two midwives, a mother and a sister, and a princess. The reader is invited to see how God’s purposes move forward even when he seems to be absent. It is a pattern you have seen before, in Joseph’s story, and in Job’s.

Pharaoh is a portrait of power that fears. He has the largest empire in the world, and he is afraid of a population of slaves. His answer is violence, first by labor and then by murder. But every plan he makes fails. The more he oppresses, the more Israel grows. The Nile that he orders the babies thrown into becomes the place where a rescuer is drawn out. The book is teaching you early that God’s promises cannot be defeated by the schemes of rulers.

The midwives are among the quiet heroes of Scripture. They “feared God” more than they feared Pharaoh. The fear of God, as you learned in Job 28:28, is the beginning of wisdom, and it is also the source of courage. They have no power, and they do something small: they let the boys live. God honors them and gives them families of their own. Their story is a reminder that obedience to God sometimes means quiet resistance to unjust authority.

Moses’ own story is full of echoes. A baby is put in a floating basket, the same word as Noah’s ark, and is saved through water. He is raised in the house of the oppressor, and he is then a fugitive. At first he tries to rescue his people by his own strength, with violence, and it fails. He needs to be taught a better way. Forty years in the wilderness will do that.

But the center of the passage is the last two verses. God hears, remembers, sees, and knows. These are four verbs, and the first three recall what God does in covenant. “Remembered his covenant” does not mean that God had forgotten. It means that he is now acting on what he promised. The slavery of Israel has not made God forget Abraham. It has set the stage for him to keep his word.
connection: Stephen retells this story in Acts 7:17-29, and Hebrews 11:23-27 praises the faith of Moses’ parents and of Moses himself. Matthew presents the infant Jesus escaping Herod’s murder of the boys in a way that echoes this chapter (Matthew 2:13-18). Paul says that God “chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27), and Moses is an early example.
application:
Think of a place where you feel powerless. Remember the midwives. A small act of faithfulness is not wasted.

Notice how often God’s actions in this story are hidden. If you are in a season where you cannot see God working, ask him to show you where he is, and trust that he has heard.

Pray for people who are living under oppression today, and ask what you could do to help.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he hears groaning and remembers his covenant.
Ask for courage to fear him more than anyone with power.
Pray for someone who is crying out today.
